Chapter 30

The globe: Threlte, on demand

three.js through Threlte — <T.Mesh> is a mesh, children attach — with coastlines from the same atlas, arcs lifted off the surface, clickable markers, a useTask flyover that follows the library’s great-circle interpolation, a MediaQuery that holds it still, and a dynamic import so three.js reaches only the people who ask for it.

By the end of this chapter

Add a 3D scene to a SvelteKit page declaratively, animate it per frame without an effect loop, respect reduced motion, and load it lazily behind a boundary.

Threlte is Svelte for three.js. <T.Mesh> is a THREE.Mesh; its attributes are the object’s properties; a geometry and a material as children become that mesh’s geometry and material. The scene is markup, and the two things that are genuinely imperative — building vertex buffers and moving a camera per frame — are the only imperative code in the file.

Loading first, because it is the decision that matters most. three.js and Threlte are the largest dependency in the project and most visits never open the globe tab, so the import is dynamic, in markup, behind a boundary: {const { default: Globe } = await import(...)}. That declaration is bare on purpose — a module is the same module however often it is asked for, so there is nothing to follow — where the page’s {const initial = $derived(await tripBySlug(slug))} follows the slug. The pending snippet shows until the chunk arrives and the failed snippet if the network does not deliver it, with a reset that tries again. failed prints the message of what it is handed, through boundaryMessage (chapter 27), because that is an App.Error — the failure after handleError in src/hooks.client.ts has put it into words, in the page’s language (chapter 15) — and not the Error the import threw. The first version tested error instanceof Error, which an App.Error never is, so it showed its fallback whatever had happened. This is the one boundary whose failure never touches the server, so it is the one chapter 46 breaks on purpose: the test drops the chunk on its way to a German page and expects “Etwas ist schiefgelaufen” and a “Neu verbinden” button. browser guards the whole thing because a WebGL scene has no server-rendered form; the server renders the loading text and nothing else.

The frame around the scene. It loads the coastlines — the same prerendered file the map reads, so the two agree about where Portugal is — and holds the state the scene does not own: whether the camera is flying, and whether the first frame has been drawn (the canvas fades in on it). Reduced motion comes from src/lib/motion/prefers.svelte.ts, which hands on the framework’s own prefersReducedMotion from svelte/motion — one MediaQuery for the whole app — and it is live: change the operating system setting and the scene stops animating without a reload. The controls are outside the boundary, which is why the end-to-end test can see the button before the chunk has loaded. The hint under them is a second MediaQuery, (pointer: coarse): with a mouse a scroll wheel zooms the globe, and on a touch screen a scroll moves the page and a pinch zooms, so the sentence says pinch where a pinch is what works.

The scene

The colours first, because the first version got them wrong in an instructive way: it drew the arc in --sun and every stop in --coral, so the same route was teal on the Map tab and amber on the Globe tab next to it, and two *state* colours — warning and danger — were spent as decoration. Now the route is in the sea and each stop in its kind’s hue, exactly as on the map. They are the dark theme’s values whatever the page’s theme, because the globe is a night scene, and they are copied from tokens.css by hand, because a WebGL material cannot read a custom property — which is why GlobeStop grew a kind. A latitude and longitude become a point on the unit sphere, with 0°E facing the default camera. The coastlines become a BufferGeometry of line segments — every ring of every polygon, pairs of consecutive points — which is twenty thousand vertices and one draw call. interactivity() from @threlte/extras is what makes onclick on a mesh work: it raycasts from the pointer into the scene.

Each leg gets an arc from the library’s arc(), lifted off the surface by an amount that grows with the leg’s length so a long flight visibly arcs and a short hop hugs the ground. The geometries are built in $derived, so a change to the stops rebuilds exactly the arcs, and the $effect with a cleanup disposes the previous set — buffers are GPU memory, and a globe that leaks one per drag would not survive a planning session. The effect computes nothing a template reads; it only frees what lives outside Svelte, which is the job an effect is for. Each arc carries a name, the ids of the two stops it joins, and the {#each} in the markup keys on that name rather than on the arc’s position in the list: a stop is a row, so no two legs of one route join the same pair, and a key that identifies the leg keeps each line with its leg when a stop is inserted before it.

The flyover. useTask runs a function every frame with the time since the last one, and the function advances along the current leg by delta / seconds, puts the camera above interpolate(a, b, progress) — the library’s great-circle interpolation, so the camera follows the line it draws — and looks at the centre. The flight variables are plain lets, not $state: they change sixty times a second and nothing renders them, so making them reactive would only schedule work. Reduced motion means a change of selection is a cut, not an ease, and the flight button does not exist.

The markup. A camera with OrbitControls from extras, disabled while flying so the two do not fight; two lights; Stars for a restrained bit of cinema, with speed={0} under reduced motion; the sphere; a slightly larger back-facing shell for an atmosphere; the coastlines; the arcs; and one small mesh per stop, scaled up when selected and clickable. bind:ref={camera} hands the three.js camera to the task. Every colour here is a literal or one of the two constants above, like the map’s, because WebGL does not read the cascade; the selected stop is white, the one thing lit. The camera starts over the route — the mean of the stops as unit vectors, which is the right middle on a sphere where an average of longitudes is not — at the distance where the sphere fills about 80% of the frame’s shorter side: a sphere of radius R fills an angle of 2·asin(R/d) from a distance d, and the horizontal field of view comes from the canvas’s aspect, so a portrait phone backs the camera off instead of cutting the globe at both edges. Until the person turns the globe, a resize re-frames it; OrbitControls’ onstart is how the scene knows they have.

Why Threlte and not three.js in an attachment

The same line as the map. A scene is a tree — camera, lights, meshes, materials — and a template is a tree; Threlte maps one onto the other and {#each markers} gives you a mesh per stop for free, with disposal handled when the each block shrinks. An attachment would be the right shape for a single canvas that an imperative renderer owns end to end, and there is one of those in project 5. Here, three quarters of the scene is declarative and Threlte lets it stay that way.

Checkpoint

  • You can say why the globe is a dynamic import in markup and what the boundary’s two snippets do.
  • You can explain what useTask is and why the flight variables are not $state.
  • You know where reduced motion is honoured in this component, and by what mechanism.
